questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify the liquid in which rubidium is likely to be stored in the laboratory.

(ii) Why is rubidium stored in this liquid?

(iii) Which of the two elements (Rb and K) is more reactive?

(iv) Identify one other element belonging to the same group as Rb and K.

(v) What is the family name of this group of elements? *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Paraffin oil** (kerosene).

(ii) Rubidium reacts very vigorously with oxygen and with moisture in the air. The oil **keeps air and water out**, so the metal does not react; it is denser than the oil, so it stays covered.

(iii) **Rubidium** is more reactive: reactivity increases down Group I because the single outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily.

(iv) Any one of: **lithium, sodium, caesium** (francium).

(v) The **alkali metals**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Write the formula of the oxide of rubidium and state its acid base property.

Formula of oxide: ................

Acid base property: ................ *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Rubidium forms the ion $\mathrm{Rb^+}$ and oxygen forms $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, so the formula of the oxide is **$\mathrm{Rb_2O}$**.

Acid base property: it is a **basic oxide** (it reacts with water to give the alkaline solution $\mathrm{RbOH}$: $\mathrm{Rb_2O} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{RbOH}$).

questions.enonce_markdown: Write a chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of rubidium nitrate ($\mathrm{RbNO_3}$). *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Like potassium nitrate, rubidium nitrate gives the nitrite and oxygen when heated:

$2\mathrm{RbNO_3} \xrightarrow{\;\text{heat}\;} 2\mathrm{RbNO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$

Check: Rb 2 = 2; N 2 = 2; O 6 = 4 + 2.

questions.enonce_markdown: State a method by which rubidium can be extracted from its ore. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown: **Electrolysis of molten (fused) rubidium chloride**: rubidium ions gain electrons at the cathode, $\mathrm{Rb^+} + e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Rb}$, and chlorine is given off at the anode. (The metal is too reactive to be obtained by reducing its oxide with carbon.)
